name: Gareth Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead a shift of industrial fabric looms at the mill. I have a two-year technical diploma and set yarn tension, clear broken threads and check the first roll under a light table. A clean fabric run is satisfying; lifting a jammed yarn beam after a night shift is the rough part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a bakery, and we have no children. We have about nine months of expenses saved and are putting money aside for a flat. I earn a higher lead rate, and plenty of nearby mills have similar jobs. I use AI now and then to shorten fault notes, but always compare them with the machine log and the fabric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our weaving shift the AI fault summaries are sometimes useful, but the looms still have to make fabric without weak stripes. A tidy report does not tighten a loose warp thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn a higher lead rate, and my partner and I have about nine months of expenses saved. Nearby mills advertise similar work. If the change stays small, our paid shifts and the flat we're saving for still look manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting up the industrial fabric looms and checking the first roll with the light table. I'll use AI now and then to shorten a fault note, as I already do, then compare it with the machine log. I'll add some new money from each wage to the flat account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The pay keeps coming, and the fault note remains something I can check against cloth I can touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the machine log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the summary said a thread break lasted one minute, but the meter showed a longer weak section. We cut that length out instead of shipping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide what to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner manages a bakery and has early starts. We compare savings on Sunday evenings, after both shifts are done, and decide how much of each new wage can go toward the flat.

say: **AI fault notes** can help, but the cloth and meter decide what ships.
The **weaving crew** still checks weak stripes and thread tension.
think: Our **lead wage** and the bakery income continue in the mild case.
Nine months of **savings** give us a strong base for a flat.
do: **Keep** setting looms and checking first rolls on the light table.
**Add** new money from each wage to the flat account.
feel: **Calm** about secure mill work and checked paperwork help.
S0.quote: A tidy report does not tighten a loose warp thread.
fieldNote: Gareth already uses **AI occasionally** for notes but verifies them against cloth and meter readings.
A **higher lead rate** and nine-month reserve support calm and ongoing flat saving.

steps.text: Keep setting industrial fabric looms and checking first rolls
Add new money from each lead-rate wage to flat savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI may book yarn and spot order errors before it changes the loom itself. If the mill wants a faster schedule, the union should be in the room when checking time is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some change to planning and the office, but the fabric still has to be woven and inspected by us for now. My own pay seems safe. I'd take a proven control tool if it lets me find a thread break without adding an unpaid task at the end of shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the production lead for a paid supervised session on the new fault-pattern screen, if the mill offers one. Once offered, I'll learn its correction controls on one stopped loom and compare five rolls with the light table. I'll join the union shift meeting to ask that checking time stays on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about speed becoming a target, though I do not expect to lose my own wage in this slower change. I want evidence from actual rolls before I trust a coloured screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a screen trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test must run on a stopped loom with a technician beside me, and the previous five rolls need a human quality record. I am requesting a paid supervised loom-screen session; the mill has not offered a place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a flagged stripe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the new screen flags a weak stripe, I'll mark its metre position and ask the checker to match it against the fabric. A correct mark is useful; a false alarm still costs paid inspection time.

say: **Yarn booking** may change before the hands-on weaving job does.
The **union shift meeting** should protect paid fabric checking time.
think: My own **lead wage** looks safe for now.
A **proven control tool** interests me if it finds thread breaks without adding unpaid work after my shift.
do: **Request** paid supervised access to the new loom fault screen.
**Learn** correction controls in an offered paid stopped-loom session, with a technician and five rolls backed by human records.
**Join** the union meeting about paid checking time.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed targets while current pay remains secure.
S1.quote: I am requesting a paid supervised loom-screen session; the mill has not offered a place yet.
fieldNote: The **screen session is requested**, with participation conditional on an offered paid supervised slot.
He would **learn correction controls** in paid stopped-loom practice, using five rolls with human quality records.

steps.text: Learn correction controls in offered paid technician-supervised stopped-loom session using five human-recorded rolls
Join union shift meeting about paid fabric inspection time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 might plan yarn orders, and capable robots around 2031 could thread and reset the looms. I'd tell the union to seek a written crew plan and proper stop authority before a robot handles a moving warp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 32 when the physical robots arrive. Nine months saved and plenty of local factory jobs give me options, but fewer lead shifts would still reduce the money for rent and our flat. My partner's bakery wage is helpful, not a replacement for mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask for the mill's robot timetable through the union steward. If there is an offered paid maintenance-setter course with supervised work on a locked loom and a recognized certificate, I'll attend. If the mill cuts my shifts after that, I'll apply for posted local setter jobs I qualify for with safe duties and pay that covers our costs; without a course, I'll apply for posted weaving-lead jobs at adequate pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a robot that can reset a loom could shrink my paid team. I still have the savings, the diploma and nearby plants, so I can make choices before the account runs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should practical training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer has to make us lock the loom and practise releasing a jammed yarn beam. A video of a robot threading clean fabric would not teach the stop procedure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a setter vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare a setter posting's actual hourly rate and roster with what we need for rent and the flat deposit. If it pays less than that, I'll keep the current shifts while applying elsewhere.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may plan yarn before robots thread looms around 2031.
A **written crew plan** and stop authority should precede robot changeovers.
think: At **32**, fewer lead shifts could reduce rent and flat money.
Nine months of **savings** and other local mills give time, not permanent wages.
do: **Ask** union steward for the mill robot timetable.
**Attend** paid recognized maintenance-setter training if a safe place is offered.
**Apply** for posted local setter or weaving-lead work if shifts fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic lead-shift cuts despite strong savings.
S2.quote: A video of a robot threading clean fabric would not teach the stop procedure.
fieldNote: The **paid course** requires an actual place, locked-loom practice and recognized proof.
He separately names a **qualified setter application** and a no-course weaving fallback, both pay-dependent.

steps.text: Ask union steward for written mill robot timetable
Attend recognized setter course if offered paid locked-loom practice
Apply for posted safe local setter job if qualified, shifts cut, pay sufficient
Apply if no paid course to posted local weaving-lead job with household-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI plans orders in 2031 and robots reset looms around 2034, I'd tell our crew five years is enough to test a yarn-beam change safely. The union should have a say before management counts the saved hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 35 when the capable robots reach the floor. I could build a second skill while earning the lead wage, but a job with the same title might pay less. We still hope to buy the flat, so I cannot treat training as a guarantee of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting looms and add a new amount to savings each month. If the mill offers paid release, a real place and a recognized maintenance certificate with locked-loom practice, I'll enrol next year. After qualifying, if lead hours fall, I'll apply for posted local machine-setter jobs with safe duties and pay enough for our rent and flat plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long-run team size, but the five-year lead makes a course and an honest wage comparison possible. My current paid shift is not in danger this morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the practical day look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training day should start with a loose yarn beam and show who holds the isolation key. I'd want to do the reset myself, with a trainer ready to stop the loom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the certificate be useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maintenance certificate would be useful only if a local plant advertises a real setter job at a rate our budget can use. Otherwise I'll keep the mill wage and ask again when a safe posting appears.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes yarn planning before robot loom resets around 2034.
The union should review **saved hours** before management changes the roster.
think: At **35**, I can gain a second skill while earning a lead wage.
A **certificate** matters only with a posted safe local job and enough pay.
do: **Continue** paid loom setup and add new monthly savings.
**Enrol** in a recognized maintenance course if paid release and safe practice are offered.
**Apply** for posted local setter work after qualifying if hours fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Uneasy** about future hours, with time to prepare and current pay intact.
S3.quote: The maintenance certificate would be useful only if a local plant advertises a real setter job at a rate our budget can use.
fieldNote: The **five-year runway** supports real conditional enrolment and new saving from wages.
The later **application** requires qualification, reduced hours, safe local duties and a bill-covering advertised rate.

steps.text: Keep paid loom setup and add new monthly savings
Enrol in recognized maintenance course if paid safe place offered
Apply for posted safe local setter role if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 may plan the orders, and capable robots around 2039 could run the loom changes. I'd tell our union there's time to negotiate how saved hours pay for training instead of just disappearing from the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 at the thinking-AI date and 40 when robots can do the physical work. Ten years lets my partner and me save for the flat and see which factory roles actually grow. Still, I expect to need a wage well beyond 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the lead loom work and put new wage money into our flat account each month. I'll enrol in the recognized maintenance course when a paid place with locked-loom practice is offered, then check real local vacancies each year. If robots later cut my hours, I'll apply only to posted safe jobs I qualify for with a rate that meets our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant robot date rather than the next wage packet. A decade improves our choices, but it does not make a posted job or a paid course appear by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check during a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the first robot test I would compare the tension record with the actual fabric and keep a person at the stop control. If a weak stripe appears, the roll stays on our side of the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a union agreement secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to get paid practice time and a right to stop the line into the next agreement. If the mill saves labour hours, the agreement should say how operators gain training time.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable loom robots around 2039.
The union should negotiate **paid practice** and stop authority before hours are changed.
think: At **40**, I still expect to need factory wages after robots arrive.
A **long runway** can build flat savings, though no future vacancy is guaranteed.
do: **Keep** leading the loom line and add new savings monthly.
**Enrol** in paid recognized maintenance training if a safe place is offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local jobs if robots cut hours and pay fits.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robot change while current pay remains solid.
S4.quote: A decade improves our choices, but it does not make a posted job or a paid course appear by itself.
fieldNote: His **steady adaptability** favors proved trials, then a paid practical course and qualified local application.
The **strong reserve** grows from new wages; later job moves require actual cuts, safe duties and sufficient posted pay.

steps.text: Keep lead loom work and add new wage savings monthly
Enrol in maintenance course if paid recognized safe place offered
Apply for posted safe local job if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient
Seek paid practice and stop authority through union agreement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 case worries me most. Robots able to reset looms around 2031 could reduce my paid lead shifts at 32. A written roster plan, an offered paid maintenance place and a real safe local job at enough pay would let me respond before we spend the flat savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I should have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can press stop when a robot threads a loom and the fabric starts to weaken. A green screen cannot hold together a broken warp thread.

headlineQuote: A green screen cannot hold together a broken warp thread.
portrait: **Gareth**, 27, leads industrial fabric looms and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He and his bakery-manager partner have **nine months** of expenses saved and hope to buy a flat.
He uses **AI occasionally** for fault notes, checking them against fabric and the machine log.
He waits for **proved safe tools**, then seeks paid maintenance training and suitable posted work if robots cut hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable loom-reset robots around 2031, reducing his higher paid lead shifts at 32.
whatWouldHelp: A **written roster plan**, offered paid maintenance place and safe local job at enough pay would protect their flat savings.
